summary: A report from an Internet Architecture Board workshop held in March 2006 that brought together network operators, standards people, and researchers. They discussed unwanted traffic such as DDoS attacks, spam, and phishing, where it comes from, and how well existing defenses work. The report also lists engineering and research topics that might help fight it. It is informational, not a specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Grown-ups who run the internet met for two days to talk about junk and attacks online, then wrote down what they learned and what to work on next.

subtitle: What operators, vendors and researchers told the IAB about spam, DDoS and the money behind unwanted traffic.

tldr.problem: The Internet carries a lot of unwanted traffic such as DDoS attacks, spam and phishing, and the people who run networks, set standards and do research rarely compare notes on where it comes from.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB held a workshop on March 9-10, 2006, with operators, vendors and researchers, and this report summarizes what they said about sources, impact, existing defenses and what to work on next.
tldr.outcome: The report names an underground economy as the main driver, finds existing tools weak or little deployed, and recommends updates to host and router requirements and to ingress filtering. It is a summary of contributions, not a specification.

today: RFC 4948 is an Informational report from August 2007 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the views of workshop participants rather than a standard, so treat its observations as a snapshot of 2006.

sections.title: The Workshop and Its Goals
sections.content:
The IAB (Internet Architecture Board) organized an Unwanted Internet Traffic workshop at USC/ISI in Marina del Rey, CA, on March 9-10, 2006. It invited experts from the operator, vendor and research communities to discuss what kinds of unwanted traffic are seen, how bad it is, who the major sources are, which solutions work and what needs to be done.

The report says the workshop touched only the surface of some issues, and that deriving solutions is a next step for the IAB, the IETF and the IRTF. It is a summary of participants' contributions, so it is not an IAB document and the views in it do not necessarily reflect IAB positions. It specifies no protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine the people who fix the roads, the people who make the rules and the people who study traffic all sitting in one room to talk about bad drivers. That is what this meeting was.

sections.title: The Underground Economy
sections.content:
The first message of the report is that an underground economy supplies the money that drives unwanted traffic. It runs largely on IRC servers that work like shopping malls, selling stolen credit card and bank account data, malware, botnets and root access to compromised hosts. Miscreants turn this into cash through stolen accounts, purchases shipped via remailers, and money-laundering services.

The report lists four factors that feed the problem. The Internet is wide open to millions of mostly unprotected hosts. A huge number of hosts are compromised, often without their owners knowing. The Internet was designed without audit trails, so attacks are hard to trace. And the legal system lags: laws are mostly local while the traffic respects no borders.

Activity has also changed. Early bots were mostly used for easily detected DDoS attacks. Now systems are quietly subverted for future financial gain, and bots masquerade as normal user activity. The report stresses that the real threat is the criminals behind the bots, with losses counted in multiple billions of dollars.
sections.plainLanguage: Some people make real money by breaking into other people's computers and renting them out. Because it pays well and rarely gets them caught, more and more bad traffic shows up.

sections.title: How Bad Is It for Each Kind of Network
sections.content:
The workshop discussed mainly DDoS traffic and spam, and found that the impact differs by who you are.

  • Backbone providers are mostly concerned with availability. Their links are well provisioned, so a 5Gbps attack could be absorbed. Their main tools are Access Control Lists (ACLs) and BGP null routes. An informal estimate was that only about 10% of DDoS attacks are reported, and some estimates put it as low as 2%.
  • Access providers suffer most from customer support load. During the Microsoft Blaster worm attack, handling an average customer call took over an hour. Patching follows an exponential decay of roughly 40% per month, so some hosts stay vulnerable for life.
  • Enterprises sort unwanted traffic into Nuisance, Malicious and Unknown, prefer prevention to detection, and prefer false negatives to costly false positives.
  • DNS operators reported growing DDoS attacks on .com, .net and root servers, including reflection attacks using spoofed source addresses. Their only viable mitigation is over-engineering and network anycast.
sections.plainLanguage: A big highway company, a neighborhood phone helpline and a company office all get hurt by bad traffic in different ways, so each needs a different fix.

sections.title: Existing Defenses and Why They Fall Short
sections.content:
The report lists known vulnerabilities: packet source address spoofing, BGP route hijacking, moving everything over HTTP to get past firewalls, changing paths that make TTL checks unreliable for mobile hosts, network authentication that is too complex, and security tools that go unused.

The solution mentioned most at the workshop was BCP 38 (RFC 2827) on ingress filtering, whose universal deployment can block DDoS attacks that use spoofed source addresses. It is not widely deployed, because it may need device upgrades, is tedious to maintain, and gives the deploying site no direct benefit. RFC 3704 (BCP 84) extends it to multihomed networks. Unicast Reverse Path Filtering (uRPF) offers a restricted form, but asymmetric routing may force the loose test, which does not guarantee against all spoofing.

Enterprises rely on firewalls, application level gateways and anti-spam software, and computer admission control is a newer, more expensive option. The report blames inadequate tools, inadequate deployment, which is partly a lack of incentives, and inadequate education. On the question of closing off open access, the workshop reached a rough consensus that controlled access does not seem the best solution. Instead it called for risk assessment, traceability and liability.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a good rule that says every network should check where its mail-like packets claim to come from. Hardly anyone follows it because it costs them effort and mostly helps other people.

sections.title: Tools in the Pipeline, Research and Wishes
sections.content:
Vendors described ideas such as a Central Policy Repository of known-good policies, flow based tools that build a baseline of normal behavior and flag anomalies, deep packet inspection, and the Internet Motion Sensor, which watches unused address space and monitored approximately 17 million prefixes, about 1.2% of the IPv4 address space. Discussion of SHRED, which makes spam expensive for spammers, reached no agreement on its effectiveness.

On research, the report covers prevention, detection and defense for exploited hosts, application and network oriented DDoS research, forensic aids, measurements and traffic analysis. It also notes that research can be misused, for example anonymity networks and distributed hash tables.

In a session called Aladdin's Lamp, operators listed wishes: a reliable security contact in each administrative domain, organized security testing, safer default settings, automated sharing of attack information, and automatic filtering of unwanted traffic. The report says these are still wishes and their feasibility was not examined.
sections.plainLanguage: The group also asked what they would wish for if they had a magic lamp: easy ways to reach each other, safer settings out of the box and a way to share warnings fast.

sections.title: Workshop Conclusions and Recommended Steps
sections.content:
The closing session split the suggested actions into three classes. The hard questions include the role of cryptography in the architecture, how far to curtail openness and add complexity, whether core routing needs a separately managed control plane, and whether the economic substructure can change.

The medium or long term steps include tightening core routing security, cleaning up the Internet Routing Registry, taking down botnets and educating the community to use updated host, router and ingress filtering BCPs.

The immediately actionable steps recommended for the IETF are to update the host requirements (RFC 1122 and RFC 1123, from 1989), the router requirements (RFC 1812, from 1995) and the ingress filtering BCPs. The IAB should inform the community about the underground economy, and the IRTF should study it and start research on countermeasures. The Security Considerations section only notes that the document specifies no protocol or bits on the wire.
sections.plainLanguage: At the end they made a to-do list: some jobs are quick, like updating old rulebooks, and some are huge, like changing how the money side of the problem works.
